units.title: Unit 55 — Obligation, need, possibility and probability
units.source: Vocabulary study targets from published reference material; Unit 55. Page information, if available, is retained in sourceAudit.
learningObjectives: Distinguish legal responsibility, compulsory duties and optional activities, including their verb and preposition patterns.
Talk about shortages, requirements, essential needs and lack of resources with correct collocations.
Express varying degrees of likelihood, from a mere possibility to inevitability and absolute certainty.
Avoid using need of when the intended noun phrase is a need for something.

sectionsChecked: A: Obligation; liable for, obliged to, mandatory, compulsory, obligatory, optional and exempt from
B: Need, requirements, shortage and lack
C: Possibility, likelihood and certainty; common mistake with a need for

items.pt: responsável legalmente por; sujeito a arcar com
items.example: You may be liable for repair costs if you damage the rented equipment.
items.note: Formal or legalistic: responsible for paying or bearing a consequence.

items.example: The retailer is obliged to replace a faulty product under the warranty.
items.note: Obliged to do something expresses a duty imposed by rules or circumstances.

items.example: The sudden power failure forced the engineers to stop the experiment.
items.note: Force takes an object followed by to and an infinitive.

items.pt: sob a mira de uma arma
items.example: The witness said the driver had been threatened at gunpoint.
items.note: Used when someone is threatened with a gun; a particularly strong form of coercion.

items.example: With the road blocked, we had no choice but to turn back.
items.note: The fixed pattern is have no choice but to plus infinitive.

items.example: With no spare parts available, the team had no alternative but to postpone the test.
items.note: A slightly more formal equivalent of have no choice but to.

items.example: Completion of the safety course is mandatory for all laboratory visitors.
items.note: Required by a rule or law; not left to individual choice.

items.example: Attendance at the introductory session is compulsory for new employees.
items.note: Often used of education, training and activities required by rules.

items.example: Wearing a helmet is obligatory on this construction site.
items.note: Similar to compulsory; something that must be done.

items.example: The extra practice class is optional, so you can decide whether to attend.
items.note: The opposite of compulsory or mandatory; not required.

items.example: Students with a medical certificate may be exempt from the physical test.
items.note: Exempt from is followed by a noun or an -ing form.

items.example: You do not have to attend the optional workshop.
items.note: Expresses lack of obligation, not prohibition.

items.example: The old heating system is in need of urgent maintenance.
items.note: Often more formal than simply needs; the pattern is in need of something.

items.example: There is a clear need for additional training before the equipment arrives.
items.note: After the noun need, use for, not of.

items.example: The hospital reported a shortage of qualified technicians.
items.note: A shortage of means an insufficient supply, rather than a complete absence.

items.example: The prototype failed through lack of adequate cooling.
items.note: More formal than because there was not enough; lack of has no article here.

items.example: A lack of clear instructions delayed the installation.
items.note: A lack of refers to an absence or insufficient amount of something.

items.example: Reliable internet access is an absolute necessity for this remote project.
items.note: A necessity is something essential rather than merely convenient.

items.pt: não conseguir ficar sem; ser indispensável
items.example: Our team cannot do without reliable backup power during testing.
items.note: The phrasal expression means that something is essential or extremely useful.

items.example: Check the entry requirements for the postgraduate programme.
items.note: Usually plural for a list of conditions that must be met.

items.example: I was offered an opportunity to collaborate with a research group abroad.
items.note: An opportunity is a favourable, real chance to do something.

items.example: There is a chance that the meeting will finish early.
items.note: Less formal than possibility when referring to what might happen.

items.example: We should consider the possibility of a temporary network outage.
items.note: Often followed by of plus an -ing form; more formal than chance.

items.example: Some disruption is inevitable while the bridge is being repaired.
items.note: Describes something certain or impossible to avoid.

items.example: It is doubtful whether the supplier can deliver by Friday.
items.note: Often used in the pattern it is doubtful whether plus a clause.

items.example: It is probable that the new rules will take effect next year.
items.note: Probable indicates that something is more likely than not, not certain.

items.example: The exact launch date is still not an absolute certainty.
items.note: An emphatic noun phrase indicating complete certainty.

items.example: We cannot predict the outcome with certainty.
items.note: Certainty is the state of having no doubt about something.

items.example: The driver is liable if the vehicle is damaged through careless use.
items.note: Usually linked to a responsibility with liable for; do not confuse it with merely likely.

items.example: The contract creates an obligation to protect customer information.
items.note: A duty created by an agreement, rule, law or moral principle.

items.example: The team estimated the probability of a delay before planning the schedule.
items.note: A measure or judgement of how likely an event is; contrasted with possibility.

units.title: Unit 56 — Sound and light
units.source: Vocabulary study targets from published reference material; Unit 56. Page information, if available, is retained in sourceAudit.
learningObjectives: Distinguish neutral sound, negative noise and informal racket, including countable and uncountable use.
Choose specific verbs and nouns for metallic, continuous, sharp, soft, heavy and distant sounds.
Describe gloomy or dim conditions and distinguish ways light shines, flashes or moves.
Recognise figurative uses of light and darkness to describe happiness, sadness and amusement.

sectionsChecked: A: Sound, noise and racket; countability
B: Sound words and typical sources; illustrated vocabulary table
D: Light and related collocations; language-help box

items.example: The sound of running water helped me relax.
items.note: A neutral word for what we hear; can be countable or uncountable.

items.example: The noise from the building work made concentration difficult.
items.note: Usually suggests unwanted or unpleasant sound; countable for distinct noises, uncountable for continuous noise.

items.example: The neighbours were making such a racket that nobody could sleep.
items.note: Informal: a very loud, annoying mixture of sounds, often from people.

items.example: I heard several strange noises coming from the empty room.
items.note: Plural noises refers to individual sounds or kinds of sound.

items.example: Please try not to make noise while the recording is in progress.
items.note: The noun is normally uncountable when referring to unwanted sound in general.

items.example: The din from the old machinery made conversation impossible.
items.note: A loud, sustained and often unpleasant noise; useful alternative discussed in the answer key.

items.example: A sudden bang from the loading bay startled everyone.
items.note: A sharp, loud sound, such as a slamming door or bursting balloon; noun or verb.

items.example: The clock in the town square chimed at midday.
items.note: A clear musical ringing, typically from bells or a clock; noun or verb.

items.example: The metal gate clanged shut behind the cyclist.
items.note: A loud, resonant metallic sound; noun or verb.

items.example: The dishes clattered as the waiter stacked them.
items.note: A series of hard, irregular striking sounds; noun or verb.

items.example: A heavy box crashed to the warehouse floor.
items.note: A sudden loud noise caused by a collision or fall; noun or verb.

items.example: Steam hissed from the valve when the pressure rose.
items.note: A long, sharp sound made by escaping air, gas or steam; noun or verb.

items.example: The fan hummed quietly as the computer started.
items.note: A continuous low sound, often from an electrical machine; noun or verb.

items.example: Loose screws rattled inside the toolbox.
items.note: Repeated short hard sounds made by shaking or vibration; noun or verb.

items.example: The alarm rang just as the meeting began.
items.note: Used for bells, alarms and telephones; noun or verb.

items.example: We could hear the roar of the waterfall from the path.
items.note: A very loud, powerful and sustained noise; noun or verb.

items.example: Thunder rumbled in the distance before the storm arrived.
items.note: A deep, continuous, often distant sound; noun or verb.

items.example: Dry leaves rustled under our shoes.
items.note: A soft sound made by moving leaves, paper or light material; noun or verb.

items.example: The tyres screeched when the driver braked suddenly.
items.note: A very high-pitched, piercing sound; noun or verb.

items.example: The heavy parcel landed on the rug with a thud.
items.note: A dull, heavy impact sound, often on a soft surface; noun or verb.

items.pt: tamborilar leve; som de batidas rápidas
items.example: Rain pattered against the kitchen window all evening.
items.note: Repeated light, quick tapping sounds; noun or verb.

items.example: The narrow room felt gloomy even in the afternoon.
items.note: For places, dark and depressing; for people, unhappy or pessimistic.

items.example: The corridor was dim because only one ceiling light worked.
items.note: Light that is not bright, or something difficult to see clearly.

items.example: They chose sombre colours for the formal ceremony.
items.note: British spelling; conveys seriousness or a dark, imposing atmosphere.

items.example: A beam of light from the torch crossed the dark room.
items.note: A concentrated shaft of light, often from a torch or spotlight.

items.pt: um clarão; um lampejo de luz
items.example: A brief flash of light revealed the distant tower.
items.note: A sudden burst of light that lasts a very short time.

items.pt: cintilar; brilhar com pontos de luz
items.example: The glass decorations sparkled beneath the ceiling lights.
items.note: To shine with many small, bright points; often used of gems and water.

items.example: Stars twinkled above the campsite after sunset.
items.note: To shine with small, changing points of light, especially stars.

items.example: The candle flickered whenever the window was opened.
items.note: Light that varies or moves unsteadily; especially a flame or an unstable lamp.

items.example: The embers glowed long after the main fire had gone out.
items.note: To give a steady, often soft light; also metaphorical for happiness.

items.example: The morning sun shone through the curtains.
items.note: A general verb for giving or reflecting light; past shone when giving light.

items.example: The first rays of light reached the valley at dawn.
items.note: Individual lines or streams of light, especially from the sun.

items.example: The metal surface glittered after it had been polished.
items.note: To shine with repeated small bright reflections; often of gold or other shiny material.

items.example: The emergency lamp can give out light for several hours.
items.note: Give out means emit or produce light, heat or another substance.

items.example: Her face glowed with pleasure when she heard the good news.
items.note: Figurative glow describes a visibly happy expression.

items.example: He looked gloomy after learning that the trip had been cancelled.
items.note: A person's expression can be gloomy, not just a room or sky.

items.example: She beamed at her colleague after the successful presentation.
items.note: To smile broadly and happily at someone; appears in the exercise vocabulary.

items.example: There was a twinkle in his eyes as he revealed the surprise.
items.note: A metaphor for an expression of amusement, delight or humour.
